questions.q: What is the difference between a function declaration `function greet() {}` and a function expression `const greet = function() {}` in terms of hoisting?
questions.a: A function declaration is fully hoisted (name and body), so it can be called before its definition in the code. A function expression is not hoisted — only the variable declaration (`const greet`) is hoisted (in TDZ for `const`/`let`), so calling `greet()` before the line throws a ReferenceError. A wrong answer (e.g., "both are hoisted the same way") reveals the student confuses declaration vs expression semantics, leading to runtime errors when reordering code.

questions.q: Explain why `btn.onclick = handleClick` and `btn.addEventListener('click', handleClick)` behave differently when you want to attach two separate click handlers to the same button.
questions.a: `onclick` is a single property — assigning a second handler overwrites the first. `addEventListener` allows multiple handlers for the same event on the same element; they execute in registration order. A wrong answer (e.g., "both allow multiple handlers") shows the student doesn't understand the DOM Level 0 vs Level 2 event model, causing silent bugs where only the last-assigned handler runs.

questions.q: Write a function `validateAge(input)` that returns `true` if the input value is a number between 18 and 60 inclusive, otherwise `false`. Then show how to attach it to an `<input id="age">` so that the border turns red on invalid input when the user leaves the field.

Compare arrow functions `() => {}` and regular functions `function() {}` in the context of `this` binding inside an event handler. Why does `btn.addEventListener('click', () => { console.log(this); })` log `window` (or global) while `btn.addEventListener('click', function() { console.log(this); })` logs the button element?
questions.a: Arrow functions do not have their own `this`; they capture `this` lexically from the enclosing scope (here, the global scope). Regular functions bind `this` to the element on which the listener is registered (the button) when called as an event handler. A wrong answer (e.g., "both log the button") shows the student misses lexical `this` capture, causing bugs when using arrow functions as methods or event handlers needing `this`.

questions.q: A student writes `<button onclick="submitForm()">Submit</button>` and `function submitForm(event) { event.preventDefault(); ... }`. The form still submits and reloads the page. Diagnose the error and fix it without changing the HTML.
questions.a: The inline handler `onclick="submitForm()"` does not pass the event object to the function. Inside `submitForm`, `event` is `undefined`, so `event.preventDefault()` throws TypeError and the default submit proceeds. Fix: change HTML to `onclick="submitForm(event)"` OR (better) remove inline handler and use `document.querySelector('form').addEventListener('submit', submitForm)`. A wrong diagnosis (e.g., "preventDefault doesn't work on submit") reveals ignorance of event object propagation in inline handlers.
